673.title: Be a renunciant at home
673.hook: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa: make your home your forest, your heart your hermitage (Dasam, Ramkali Patshahi 10)
673.howItsDone: Sikhs sing re man aiso kar sanniaasaa in kirtan as a picture of the householder's path: detachment and devotion lived inside family and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grant me this, and your line: never turn from good. Did you do the good deed you chose, even when the moment to back out came? Today, the Tenth Guru again, this time on where a spiritual life is lived. Day six hundred seventy-three.

Everyone has had the fantasy. Quit the job, sell the stuff, move to a cabin in the mountains, and finally become the calm, deep person you'd be if life would just leave you alone. In India, that dream has an old and honored form: the sannyasi, the renunciant who leaves home for the forest, with matted hair and ashes on the skin. Guru Gobind Singh wrote a shabad that takes every piece of that picture, one by one, and moves it indoors. Today: be a renunciant at home.
screen: `THE CABIN IN THE MOUNTAINS.` → `THE SANNYASI IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERY PIECE MOVED INDOORS.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, among the Tenth Guru's hymns in the Dasam Granth. It opens: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa. In paraphrase: O mind, practice renunciation like this. Think of your whole house as the forest, and stay detached inside your own heart. Then it goes through the renunciant's kit, item by item, and gives each one a new meaning. Make self-control your matted hair. Make union with God your daily bath. Let your teacher be wisdom, and smear the Name on yourself like ashes. Eat little, sleep little, love mercy and forgiveness. Keep a gentle, contented nature, and stay free of lust, anger, greed and attachment. It's a clever move. The shabad doesn't mock the renunciant. It takes the forest life seriously, and then says the real forest is a way of living, and you can carry it into a kitchen. That's a deep thread in Sikh teaching, running back to Guru Nanak. The Gurus were householders, with families, farms and work, and they taught that God is found in the middle of ordinary life, not by escaping it. The word for the inner detachment here is udaas: unattached, free inside. You can be udaas in a crowded house, and caught in a quiet cave. So the question isn't where you live. It's whether, in the middle of the noise, there's a small clearing inside you where the Name is remembered.
screen: `O MIND, RENOUNCE LIKE THIS.` · `YOUR HOUSE IS THE FOREST.` · `THE KIT, GIVEN NEW MEANING.` · `A CLEARING IN A FULL HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE FOREST AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make your room a hermitage for a minute. Stay exactly where you are; don't tidy anything. Let the room be the forest. Notice its sounds as if they were birds and wind: the fridge, traffic, someone in the next room. Sit as still as a hermit would. Feel your feet as rooted. If you pray, you can say Waheguru in the clearing you've made. The bell holds the time.
Be a renunciant at home. The Tenth Guru's shabad: think of your house as the forest, stay unattached within, and wear self-control, mercy and the Name as the hermit's marks.
screen: `BE A RENUNCIANT AT HOME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the forest at home. Today, find one minute of stillness in the busiest room you're in, and keep it to yourself. Day six hundred seventy-three.

674.title: Songs of mourning
674.hook: Guru Nanak's dirges are sung for the dead, remembering that all must go (Vadhans M1, ang 578)
674.howItsDone: At Sikh funerals and in the days after, families gather for kirtan, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas, and Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung, in place of the old custom of ritual wailing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, be a renunciant at home, and your line: the forest at home. Did you find a minute of stillness in a busy room? This part of the path has sung for weddings and births. Today it sings at the other turning point. Day six hundred seventy-four.

In old Punjab, when someone died, the women of the village gathered in the courtyard. They sat in a circle and wailed, a lament with a rhythm to it, one woman leading, the others answering, beating their chests. The custom was called siapa, and the lament songs were alaahnees. Some families even hired professional mourners to lead them. Grief was loud, public, and shaped by tradition. Guru Nanak knew those songs. And he did something unexpected with them: he wrote his own. Today: songs of mourning.
screen: `WOMEN GATHERED IN A COURTYARD.` → `A LAMENT WITH A RHYTHM.` → `GURU NANAK WROTE HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, his laments, are in Raag Vadhans, starting on Ang five seventy-eight. He kept the form people knew, but changed what it sang about. The first one begins, in paraphrase: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. When the measure of a life is full, the soul is taken, and loved ones cry out. The body and soul are parted when the days are done. Notice the first word. A mourning song that opens with blessed. It doesn't deny the grief; the hymn says plainly that the family weeps. But it sets the grief inside something larger: a Creator who gives each life its span. Then the refrain-like truth that runs through these songs: everyone who comes must go. The king and the beggar, the young and the old. It's not said to scold anyone for crying. It's said the way a friend at a funeral says, gently, this is the road we all walk. Sikh practice took this to heart. At a Sikh funeral, the family doesn't hire mourners or beat their chests. Kirtan is sung, often Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and the Ardas is said. Many families hold a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib in the days after. The alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung. Grief is allowed. But it's held in praise, and in the plain, shared knowledge that this is how every life goes.
screen: `ALAAHNEES: THE OLD LAMENTS.` · `A DIRGE THAT OPENS WITH BLESSED.` · `EVERYONE WHO COMES MUST GO.` · `GRIEF HELD IN PRAISE.` · then, large: `ALL MUST GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone gently. Sit, and bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, even a pet. Don't reach for the hardest memory. Let an ordinary one come: their laugh, a meal, a phrase they used. Let any sadness be there too. Then, quietly, give thanks that they were given the days they had. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Alaahnee. A lament, the old Punjabi mourning song. Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa keep its form but open with praise, and remember that everyone who comes must go.
Your line: all must go. Today, tell someone you love one thing you're glad about in them, while you're both here. Day six hundred seventy-four.

675.title: The death of the brave
675.hook: death is the right of the brave, if it is accepted in the Lord's court (Vadhans M1, ang 579)
675.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa at funerals and remembrances, and these lines on the death of the brave are often recalled when martyrs are remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alaahnee, and your line: all must go. Did you tell someone one thing you're glad about in them? Today, the next lament asks a harder question: if all must go, how? Day six hundred seventy-five.

People who work in hospice sometimes say the same thing: there's a difference between someone who dies afraid and someone who dies ready. Not braver in the movie sense. Just settled. They've said what they needed to say. They've made their peace. Most of us don't like to think about it at all. We change the subject, knock on wood, scroll past. Guru Nanak's second lament doesn't change the subject. It says there's such a thing as a good death, and it says who gets one. Today: the death of the brave.
screen: `DYING AFRAID, OR DYING READY.` → `WE CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` → `A LAMENT THAT DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: The second of Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, on Ang five seventy-nine, has a line Sikhs know well. In paraphrase: death is the right of the brave, of true heroes, if their death is accepted. And nearby: don't call death bad, people, if one knows how to truly die. The word for the brave is sooraa, a hero, a warrior. But look who the hymn says the heroes are. In paraphrase again: they alone are called brave who receive honor in the true court. They leave with honor, and are honored when they arrive. So bravery here isn't measured by the battlefield. It's measured by acceptance in the dargah, the Lord's court. What makes a death accepted? The hymn's answer, and the Granth's answer everywhere, is a life lived remembering the Name, serving, honest. The death of the brave is the end of a brave life: one that didn't flinch from truth. That's why these lines mean so much to a community with many martyrs. Sikhs remember Guru Arjan, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's sons, and countless others who faced death without giving up their faith. But the hymn belongs just as much to a grandmother dying in her bed, having lived kindly and remembered God. Her death, too, is the death of the brave. One more word: parvaan, accepted, approved, signed off. It's the key to the line. The question isn't how you die. It's whether the life it ends is accepted.
screen: `DON'T CALL DEATH BAD.` · `SOORAA: WHO THE BRAVE ARE.` · `HONORED IN THE TRUE COURT.` · `PARVAAN: ACCEPTED.` · then, large: `ACCEPTED IN HIS COURT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live one brave hour. Sit, and think of the next hour of your day. What would it look like lived bravely, in this hymn's sense? Not dramatic. Just true: the honest answer, the patient word, the thing you've been avoiding. Choose one. Picture yourself doing it calmly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and ask to live this hour in a way that would be accepted. The bell holds the time.
The death of the brave. Guru Nanak's lament: death is the right of the brave, if it's accepted in the Lord's court; don't call death bad, if one knows how truly to die.
screen: `THE DEATH OF THE BRAVE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: accepted in his court. Today, do one brave, true thing in a single hour, and let that hour be enough. Day six hundred seventy-five.

screen: `DAY 675 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SHABAD FOR YOUR HOME.`

676.title: A shabad for your home
676.hook: many families have a shabad they keep for their house
676.howItsDone: Many Sikh families keep a favorite shabad for their home: framed by the door, sung at bedtime or on family occasions, often first heard at a house blessing with Sukhmani Sahib and Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the death of the brave, and your line: accepted in his court. Did you live one brave, true hour? We've sung through weddings and funerals. Today the shabads come home, to an ordinary house on an ordinary day. Day six hundred seventy-six.

Walk into some Sikh homes and you'll see it before you hear it: a framed line of Gurmukhi by the front door, or above the stove, or in the hallway. Ask about it, and you'll often get a story. It was my grandmother's favorite. My dad sang it when we moved from Kenya. We played it the night the baby came home. Families have songs the way they have recipes, passed down without anyone deciding to. In many Sikh households, one of those songs is a shabad. Today: a shabad for your home.
screen: `A FRAMED LINE BY THE DOOR.` → `EVERY LINE HAS A STORY.` → `SONGS PASSED DOWN LIKE RECIPES.`

segments.voice: Shabad means word, and in Sikh life it means a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word sung. There's no rule that a family must have one shabad of its own. But many do, and it happens in ordinary ways. A house is blessed with a reading of Sukhmani Sahib and an Ardas when a family moves in, and one line from that day sticks. A grandmother hums the same hymn every evening for forty years, and her grandchildren hum it without knowing the words. A parent sings one to a child at bedtime, and it becomes theirs. Some families keep a line many households love, like dukh bhanjan teraa naam. In paraphrase, it says: Your Name destroys pain. That shabad of Guru Arjan, on Ang two eighteen, goes on: meditate on it all day and night; the pain of the mind is gone. Others choose taatee vaao na lagaee, the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Anand Sahib's opening joy. Why does it matter? Because a household shabad works like a family's memory. It's there at the birthday and at the hospital, sung in the car and over the dishes. When something hard happens, nobody has to search for words. The words are already in the house, worn smooth by use. And there's a deeper Sikh idea underneath: the Guru isn't kept only in the gurdwara. The Word can live where you live, in the kitchen and the hallway, sung by people in their socks.
screen: `SHABAD: THE WORD, SUNG.` · `HOW A FAMILY GETS ITS HYMN.` · `DUKH BHANJAN: YOUR NAME ENDS PAIN.` · `THE WORD LIVES WHERE YOU LIVE.` · then, large: `OUR SHABAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a shabad for your home. Sit, and think back over the lines you've met on this path. Which one would you want in your house: by the door, at bedtime, on a hard day? Maybe a line from the laavan, maybe the hot wind, maybe the Name that ends pain. Let one rise. Say its words, or its meaning, silently, as if you were saying it in your own kitchen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after it. The bell holds the time.
A shabad for your home. The hymn a family keeps: sung at birthdays and hospital beds, passed down like a recipe, so the words are already there when they're needed.
screen: `A SHABAD FOR YOUR HOME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: our shabad. Today, write the line you chose somewhere in your home where you'll see it, or share it with someone you live with. Day six hundred seventy-six.

677.title: How ragis choose
677.hook: the singers choose shabads for the hour, the season and the occasion
677.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragi jathas sing kirtan through the day, choosing shabads by raag, hour, season and occasion, such as Asa di Var at dawn and the laavan at weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shabad for your home, and your line: our shabad. Did you write your line somewhere you'll see it? Today, the people who choose the shabads for everyone else. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

A good DJ reads the room. Slow songs late, upbeat ones when people walk in, nothing sad at a birthday. A ragi does something like that, with far older rules and far higher stakes. Sit in a gurdwara at four in the morning, at noon, and at sunset, and you'll hear different music each time. Go on a wedding day and on the day of a funeral, and the shabads change again. Someone is choosing. Today: the ragi.
screen: `A DJ READS THE ROOM.` → `DAWN, NOON, SUNSET SOUND DIFFERENT.` → `SOMEONE IS CHOOSING.`

segments.voice: A ragi is a singer of kirtan, Gurbani set to music. The word comes from raag, the melodic framework of Indian classical music. Ragis usually sing in a small group, a jatha, often two or three people with harmoniums and a tabla. Behind them stretches a long line: Bhai Mardana played the rabab beside Guru Nanak, and the Gurus kept musicians at their courts. The Guru Granth Sahib itself is arranged by raag. After the opening prayers, its hymns are grouped into thirty-one main raags, from Sri Raag to Jaijavanti. Each raag has a mood, and in the Indian tradition, many have a time of day or a season. So a ragi chooses on three levels. The hour: at dawn, gurdwaras sing Asa di Var in Raag Asa; in the evening, other raags and the Rehras. The season: Basant, the spring raag, is sung in its season, and Malhar, the raag of rain, comes into its own in the monsoon. And the occasion: the laavan in Raag Suhi for a wedding, the alaahneeaa in Vadhans for mourning, a shabad of comfort when the sangat is grieving. Then there's the moment itself. A good ragi listens to the room, to the news of the week, to who's sitting there. That's the real skill: not only singing beautifully, but knowing which Word this sangat needs to hear today. Sikhs say the Guru speaks through the shabad. The ragi's choice is how it arrives at the right time.
screen: `RAGI: A SINGER OF KIRTAN.` · `THE GRANTH, ARRANGED BY RAAG.` · `THE HOUR, THE SEASON, THE DAY.` · `THE WORD THIS SANGAT NEEDS.` · then, large: `THE RIGHT SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask a ragi, or read about one. Before you do, sit for the bell. Notice the hour you're in: morning, afternoon, night. Notice the season outside. Notice your own mood. Then ask yourself, as a ragi would: what kind of song does this moment need? Gentle, joyful, steady? Hold the answer. After the bell, if you know a ragi, ask how they choose; or look up a ragi jatha and read how they learned. If you pray, you can say Waheguru first. The bell holds the time.
Ragi. A singer of kirtan, who chooses the shabad for the hour, the season and the occasion, and listens for what the sangat needs.
Your line: the right song. Today, before you put music on, pause and ask what this hour needs, then choose for that. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

678.title: Learning one by heart
678.hook: learning one shabad by heart means it's there when you need it
678.howItsDone: Many Sikhs learn their daily prayers and favorite shabads by heart, often as children repeating after a parent or grandparent, so they can recite them anywhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ragi, and your line: the right song. Did you pause before choosing music, and ask what the hour needed? A ragi knows hundreds of shabads. Today, the gift of knowing just one. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

Think how many phone numbers you knew by heart twenty years ago, and how many you know now. Maybe two. We've handed our memory to our pockets, and mostly that's fine. Until the battery dies at the wrong moment. The same thing is true of words that steady us. A line saved in an app is no help in an MRI machine, or at three in the morning, or in the half second before you say something you'll regret. Only what's inside you is there then. Today: learning one by heart.
screen: `PHONE NUMBERS WE USED TO KNOW.` → `MEMORY HANDED TO OUR POCKETS.` → `ONLY WHAT'S INSIDE IS THERE.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi, to learn something by heart is to make it kanth, literally, to put it in the throat. It's a lovely image: the words live where your voice comes from, ready to rise. For centuries, this is how Gurbani lived for most Sikhs. Before printing, few families owned a handwritten copy of the scripture, and many couldn't read. So people carried it kanth. Children learned the Japji Sahib by repeating it after a grandparent each morning. Many Sikhs today still know their daily prayers by heart, the Nitnem you've met this year: Japji, Jaap, the Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras, Sohila. Some know long hymns like Sukhmani Sahib. And the Granth itself treats the Word as something held inside. Guru Amar Das says, on Ang sixty-seven, in paraphrase: the Guru's bani is the light in this world; by grace it comes to dwell in the mind. That's the hope: not words you look up, but words that live in you. Learning by heart changes how a shabad works. Read on a page, it's information. Known by heart, it's company. It comes back on its own while you're driving or washing up, and each time you understand a little more. Old Sikh teachers say a line truly learned keeps teaching for a lifetime. You don't need a whole bani to start. Two lines, really known, are enough to be there when you need them.
screen: `KANTH: KEPT IN THE THROAT.` · `HOW GURBANI LIVED BEFORE PRINT.` · `THE BANI IS LIGHT IN THE MIND.` · `TWO LINES, REALLY KNOWN.` · then, large: `BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn two lines by heart. Choose your two lines: the shabad you picked for your home two days ago, or any line from this path. Say the first line aloud, slowly, three times. Close your eyes and say it once without looking. Then the second line, the same way. Then both together. If you lose a word, peek and try again; no rush. If you pray, you can let the lines be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Learning one by heart. To make a shabad kanth, kept in the throat, so the words are inside you, ready, when there's no book and no phone.
Your line: by heart. Today, say your two lines three more times, once in the morning, once at noon, once before sleep, without looking. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

679.title: Singing it for someone
679.hook: a shabad sung for a sick or grieving friend is a gift
679.howItsDone: When someone is ill or has died, Sikh families and friends often gather at home for Sukhmani Sahib, kirtan and Ardas, singing shabads of comfort for the person and the family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, learning one by heart, and your line: by heart. Did your two lines stay with you? It's the end of a week that made the forest at home, sang laments, honored the brave, kept a shabad for the house, chose the right song and learned it by heart. Today: give it away. Day six hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `THE FOREST AT HOME · ALL MUST GO · ACCEPTED · OUR SHABAD · THE RIGHT SONG · BY HEART.`

segments.voice: When someone we love is sick or grieving, we tend to freeze. What do you say to a friend whose father just died? What do you bring to a hospital room? Flowers wilt, food piles up, and words come out wrong. Many Sikh families have an answer older than any of that. They sit by the bed, or in the living room of the grieving house, and they sing. Not performers. Aunties, cousins, a neighbor with a harmonium. Today: singing it for someone.

segments.voice: In Sikh life, a shabad can be a gift you give with your voice. When someone is ill, families often gather for a reading of Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace, or for kirtan at home, and end with an Ardas asking for the person's wellbeing. When someone has died, the sangat gathers at the family's house in the days that follow, for readings and kirtan, so the family isn't alone with the silence. What gets sung? Often a shabad of comfort. One line many families turn to in illness comes from Sukhmani Sahib, on Ang two seventy-four. In paraphrase: the Name is the medicine for every illness. Others sing the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Name that destroys pain. Why singing, and not just talking? A few reasons Sikhs give. First, the words aren't yours. You don't have to find the perfect thing to say; the Guru has already said it. Second, singing is shared. The sick person can listen with their eyes closed, and nobody has to make conversation. Third, it carries something beyond the singer. Sikhs believe the shabad is the Guru's own voice, so singing it for someone is offering them the Guru's company, not just your own. And here's the quiet part: it doesn't have to be good. A wobbly voice, a phone playing a recording, a line whispered at a bedside. The gift is the attention, and the Word.
screen: `A GIFT GIVEN WITH YOUR VOICE.` · `SUKHMANI AND KIRTAN AT HOME.` · `THE NAME, MEDICINE FOR ILLNESS.` · `IT DOESN'T HAVE TO BE GOOD.` · then, large: `SING IT FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing or send one. Sit and think of someone who's sick, tired or grieving right now. Picture their face. Then take your two lines from yesterday, or any line you love, and say or hum them softly, as if for that person. Don't worry how it sounds. After the bell, if it feels right, send them the line, a recording, or just a note saying you thought of them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Singing it for someone. A shabad given to a sick or grieving friend: the Guru's words, offered with your own voice, however it sounds.
Your line: sing it for them. Today, send one line of comfort to someone who's having a hard time, in words that aren't yours. Day six hundred seventy-nine.
